planting.note: Direct sow after all frost danger has passed and soil has warmed; this is one of the fastest-maturing dry beans available, letting northern gardeners harvest a dry crop even in short seasons.

directions: Sow seeds an inch deep directly in the garden once the soil has warmed, thinning plants to four to six inches apart in rows. King of the Early is a compact bush bean prized by Northeastern and Midwestern growers for reaching dry-bean maturity well ahead of most other shelling varieties, making it a reliable choice where the frost-free window is short. Let pods dry fully on the plant until they rattle, then shell and store the plump white beans in an airtight container. The beans cook up tender and mild, making a good all-purpose soup or baking bean.

planting.note: Sow in blocks in fertile, hilled soil; this soft flour corn needs the full warm season to fill out its large, starchy kernels and should dry fully on the stalk before harvest.

directions: Plant in blocks of several rows, hilling soil slightly around the base of the stalks as they grow for stability. Tuscarora White is a traditional soft flour corn grown by the Tuscarora Nation, one of the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy centered historically in present-day New York, and documented in American agricultural writing since the colonial period for its large, chalky-white kernels. The soft starch content makes the kernels especially suited to hominy and parching, as well as fine grinding into flour. Let ears cure fully on the stalk through fall before harvesting and shelling.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost; this is one of the earliest tomatoes available, bred specifically for short northern growing seasons.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant to the garden after frost danger passes, spacing plants about two feet apart since this is a compact determinate variety. Earliana, developed in the late 1800s and popularized by seedsmen including George Sparks of Ohio, became one of the first reliably early red tomatoes available to American gardeners and remained a market standard for decades before being supplanted by modern hybrids. The smooth, medium-sized red fruits ripen in a tight window, making this variety useful for gardeners who want an early flush of slicing tomatoes before the main-season crop comes in. Stake lightly for support and pick promptly as fruits color to extend the harvest window.
sources: William Woys Weaver: Heirloom Vegetable Gardening, Henry Holt 1997

planting.note: Direct sow in hills after last frost; this Maine-bred buttercup-type squash matures reliably within a shorter northern season than many maxima types.

directions: Sow seeds an inch deep in hills after frost danger passes, thinning to two or three vigorous plants per hill. Warren is a buttercup-type winter squash selected in Maine and long distributed through regional New England seed sources as a reliable short-season keeper. The blue-green skinned fruits hold dense, deep-orange flesh that is notably sweet and dry-textured, excellent for baking, mashing, and pies, and the fruits store well into winter when cured properly. Harvest when the rind has hardened fully and the stem begins to dry, then cure for a week or two in a warm spot before moving to cool storage.
